Enhancing anaerobic co-digestion of poultry litter and wheat straw via 
integrated microaeration, biochar, and nanoparticle strategies: Kinetic, 
microbial, and economic insights
Yuanhang Zhan a,b, Yiting Xiao a, Sarah Wu c
, Zhiwu Wang d, Jun Zhu a,*
a Department of Biological and Agricultural Engineering, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR 72701, USA
b Department of Bioproducts and Biosystems Engineering, University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN 55108, USA
c Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, University of Idaho, Moscow, ID 83844, USA
d Department of Biological Systems Engineering, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA 24060, USA
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Specific methane yield
Digestate quality
Kinetic modeling analysis
Microbial community shifts
Methanogenic functional prediction
Cost-benefit analysis
A B S T R A C T
This study systematically evaluated microaeration (M), biochar (B), and nanoparticle (N) amendments and their 
combinations for enhancing anaerobic co-digestion (Co-AD) of poultry litter with wheat straw. All strategies 
improved specific methane yield compared to the control (274.4 NmL CH4/g VS), with the biochar-nanoparticle 
combination (B+N) achieving the optimal performance (324.8 ± 3.8 NmL CH4/g VS), representing an 18.4% 
improvement. B+N achieved superior substrate degradation with 80.2% total solids and 86.3% volatile solids 
removal, exceeding the control by 38.6% and 24.2%, respectively. Kinetic modeling using the cone model and 
transfer model accurately simulated the methane production dynamics (R² > 0.9950), revealing distinct 
enhancement mechanisms. M most effectively increased the hydrolysis rate by 12.0% and maximum methane 
production rate by 19.5%, B enhanced ultimate methane potential, while N most effectively shortened the lag 
phase to 0.72–0.74 days. Microbial community analysis revealed the mechanistic fundamentals: all strategies 
enriched the acetoclastic methanogen Methanosaeta, with B+N achieving the highest archaeal abundance 
(approximately 2.0%). M enriched hydrolytic bacteria enhancing substrate degradation, B facilitated direct 
interspecies electron transfer (DIET) and microbial colonization while enriching syntrophic bacteria (Syntro­
phomonas, Syntrophobacter), and N supplied essential trace elements and promoted DIET between syntrophic 
partners. Cost-benefit analysis based on a simulated continuous reactor framework demonstrated that B+N 
achieved the optimal long-term economics with break-even at 90–120 days, making it most suitable for sustained 
operations. This study establishes an integrated kinetic-microbiological-economic framework for Co-AD process 
optimization, potentially providing practical guidance for industrial-scale implementation and advancing the 
circular bioeconomy through improved agricultural waste valorization.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) of agricultural wastes has emerged as a 
sustainable technology for simultaneously addressing environmental 
pollution and generating renewable energy through methane-rich 
biogas production [1,2]. The global imperative to transition toward 
circular bioeconomy models has intensified interest in AD systems that 
convert waste biomass into valuable energy while reducing greenhouse 
gas emissions from waste disposal. Anaerobic co-digestion (Co-AD) of 
animal manures with carbon-rich agricultural residues offers multiple 
advantages, including improved methane yield, enhanced process 
stability, better nutrient retention in digestate for agricultural applica­
tions, and optimized feedstock utilization compared to mono-digestion 
[3–5]. However, the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic substrates and po­
tential inhibitory compounds in animal wastes (ammonia, volatile fatty 
acids (VFAs), and hydrogen sulfide) often limit hydrolysis efficiency and 
methanogenic activity, adversely affecting process performance and 
economic viability. Advanced enhancement strategies targeting these 
metabolic bottlenecks have been developed to overcome these limita­
tions to promote Co-AD systems.
Microaeration (abbreviated as M), involving controlled dosing of 
small quantities of air or oxygen (typically <1% of biogas production)

into anaerobic reactors [6], has demonstrated potential for enhancing 
hydrolysis rates through selective enrichment of facultative anaerobic 
bacteria, improving process stability at high organic loading rates by 
preventing VFA accumulation, and mitigating hydrogen sulfide toxicity 
through partial oxidation to elemental sulfur or sulfate [7–9]. The 
introduction of facultative microorganisms under microaerobic condi­
tions can accelerate the degradation of complex organic polymers, 
particularly recalcitrant lignocellulosic materials, through enhanced 
extracellular enzyme production while maintaining overall anaerobic 
conditions favorable for methanogenesis in deeper reactor zones.
Biochar (abbreviated as B), a carbon-rich porous material produced 
through pyrolysis of biomass under oxygen-limited conditions (typically 
300–700◦C), has been increasingly utilized as an additive in Co-AD 
systems due to its high specific surface area, hierarchical pore struc­
ture, chemical stability, pH-buffering capacity, and unique electro­
chemical properties [10–13]. B enhances process performance through 
multiple synergistic mechanisms including providing three-dimensional 
colonization surfaces for microbial consortia that facilitate spatial or­
ganization and protection from environmental stresses, acting as a 
conductive matrix to facilitate direct interspecies electron transfer 
(DIET) between syntrophic bacteria and methanogenic archaea, 
adsorbing and sequestering inhibitory compounds such as ammonia and 
VFA to maintain favorable process conditions, promoting microbial 
aggregation and biofilm formation that enhance metabolic cooperation, 
improving nutrient retention through cation exchange capacity, and 
buffering pH fluctuations during acidogenic phases [14,15].
Nanoparticles (abbreviated as N), nano-sized materials (1–100 nm) 
with unique physicochemical properties arising from their high surface- 
area-to-volume ratios and quantum effects, represent an emerging 
strategy for Co-AD enhancement with applications spanning trace 
element supplementation, electron transfer mediation, and catalytic 
activity stimulation [16]. Metal-based N, particularly iron oxides 
(Fe3O4, Fe2O3), nickel, cobalt, and their composites, can serve as readily 
bioavailable sources of trace elements essential for methanogenic 
enzyme cofactors such as iron-sulfur clusters in hydrogenases, nickel in 
methyl-coenzyme M reductase, and cobalt in corrinoid-dependent 
methyltransferases [17,18]. Beyond nutritional supplementation, N 
can enhance DIET through increased system conductivity, stimulate 
enzyme catalytic activity through surface interactions and enhanced 
substrate accessibility, mitigate inhibitory effects by adsorbing toxic 
compounds or altering redox conditions, and influence microbial com­
munity structure through selective pressures favoring metal-resistant 
and metal-utilizing microorganisms [19,20].
Although M, B, and N supplementation have individually demon­
strated effectiveness in enhancing AD or Co-AD performance, systematic 
comparative studies evaluating their relative efficiencies under identical 
operational conditions remain limited. Furthermore, potential syner­
gistic effects from combining these strategies, which may target com­
plementary

not been comprehensively investigated. Understanding the comple­
mentary enhancement mechanisms is critical for developing optimized, 
cost-effective strategies for industrial-scale implementation that balance 
performance improvements against operational costs and practical 
constraints. Additionally, the microbial community responses to these 
enhancement strategies, including shifts in taxonomic composition, 
functional gene expression, and syntrophic network structure, remain 
incompletely characterized, limiting mechanistic understanding and 
rational design of enhancement protocols.
This study systematically compared M, B, and ferric oxide (Fe3O4) 
nanoparticles (N) as an effective nanoparticle that could enhance the AD 
process [21,22], both individually and in their combinations, for 
enhancing batch Co-AD of poultry litter (PL) with wheat straw (WS).

Well-established empirical kinetic models were applied to all treatment 
groups using a consistent framework, enabling direct comparison of key 
parameters (e.g., methane potential, rate, and lag phase) across different 
enhancement strategies (M, B, N, and their combinations). Substrate 
degradation efficiency was evaluated through total solids (TS) and 
volatile solids (TVS) removal, providing insights into organic matter 
conversion. Microbial community dynamics were comprehensively 
characterized using high-throughput 16S rRNA gene sequencing to 
elucidate taxonomic composition, with focused analysis of archaeal 
populations and predicted methanogenic pathways. Cost-benefit anal­
ysis based on a simulated continuous anaerobic sequencing batch 
reactor (ASBR) framework evaluated economic viability. Unlike previ­
ous studies that typically examine these approaches individually or in 
limited combinations, this work evaluated single, binary, and ternary 
configurations under consistent conditions, enabling direct comparison 
of their interaction effects. This approach provided a more compre­
hensive understanding of how these strategies independently and 
collectively influenced different stages of the Co-AD process, as reflected 
by process performance, kinetic behavior, and microbial community 
dynamics. The findings offer practical guidance for advancing Co-AD 
technology toward sustainable waste valorization and renewable en­
ergy production, contributing to circular bioeconomy development and 
climate change mitigation through enhanced bioenergy recovery from 
agricultural waste.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrates, inoculum, biochar, and Fe3O4 nanoparticles
Poultry litter (PL) was collected from the poultry house beddings on 
a poultry farm (University of Arkansas - Applied Broiler Research Farm, 
AR, US). The raw wheat straw (WS) was collected from a university grass 
farm (Agricultural Research & Extension Center, AR, US). The raw 
substrates were mechanically cut separately into small pieces, using two 
identical grinders (Food Processor, Hamilton Beach, Inc., VA, US). The 
results of the physicochemical properties of the pretreated PL and WS 
are shown in Table 1. As shown, PL had a relatively lower carbon-to- 
nitrogen ratio (C/N, 8) than WS (50). Thus, the mixing of PL and WS 
could formulate a co-substrate with a designed balanced C/N ratio with 
a value between 8 and 50.
Biochar was manufactured by pyrolysis of wood from recycled ma­
terials by Wakefield Biochar (Columbia, USA). Fe3O4 nanoparticles used 
in this study were manufactured by SkySpring Nanomaterials, Inc 
(Houston, USA). The basic properties of the biochar and the Fe3O4 
nanoparticles are summarized in Table 1. A scanning electron micro­
scope (SEM) was used to characterize the structure of biochar and Fe3O4 
nanoparticles. The images at different magnifications, including 500μm, 
100μm, and 50μm for biochar and 1μm, 500 nm, and 100 nm for Fe3O4 
nanoparticles, are depicted in Fig. S1. SEM images revealed that the 
biochar possesses a well-developed porous, honeycomb-like structure 
with interconnected channels, providing a high surface area for micro­
bial attachment and material immobilization. Fe3O4 nanoparticles 
exhibit a relatively uniform, near-spherical morphology with consistent 
particle sizes and form homogeneously distributed aggregates without 
pronounced size heterogeneity.
The microbial inoculum sludge collected from a laboratory-scale 
anaerobic digester was first sieved through a 1.40 mm mesh to 
remove coarse particles. The sieved sludge was subsequently pre- 
incubated at 35 ± 2 ◦C or two weeks until biogas production became 
negligible, indicating exhaustion of readily biodegradable substrates 
and minimizing background methane interference. After pre-treatment, 
the sludge was stored in a tightly sealed, opaque container at 0◦C and 
later used as the microbial inoculum for the Co-AD experiments. The 
main characteristics of the inoculum sludge are presented in Table 1.

2.2. Experimental design and methodology
This study systematically evaluated M, B, and N, both individually 
and in combinations, for enhancing batch Co-AD of PL with WS. Eight 
experimental groups were established: control with no enhancement 
(C), single-strategy treatments (M, B, N), dual-strategy combinations 
(M+B, M+N, B+N), and triple-strategy integration (M+B+N). The 
operational conditions for each enhancement strategy were optimized 
based on previous experiments and established literature recommen­
dations [23–25], as summarized in Table 2. M was implemented by 
slowly injecting a controlled volume of air into batch reactors daily 
(1.04 mL per day) for the first 4 consecutive days using a syringe to 
maintain microaerobic conditions while preserving overall anaerobic 
metabolism. B and N were added with the substrate at reactor initiali­
zation to ensure immediate availability throughout the digestion pro­
cess. Each treatment group was conducted in duplicate to ensure 
statistical reliability and obtain mean performance values. All opera­
tional parameters of the batch Co-AD process were maintained constant 
across all groups as detailed in the following section, with the applied 
enhancement strategy being the sole variable. This controlled experi­
mental design enabled rigorous comparison of treatment effects on 
process performance, including methane production and yield kinetics, 
substrate degradation efficiency (TS and VS removal), and digestate 
quality.
2.3. Batch anaerobic co-digestion operation
Identical glass containers with a total volume of 450 mL were used 
for the Co-AD process. Besides the 8 experimental groups (each in du­
plicates), blank groups (duplicates) with no substrate addition were also 
included. Duplicate reactors were employed due to the large number of 
treatment groups and practical constraints of batch Co-AD experiments. 
Preliminary trials confirmed consistent reactor performance under 
controlled conditions, and the observed small standard deviations 
indicated good reproducibility. Nevertheless, the use of duplicates might 
limit statistical robustness, and the results were interpreted with 
caution. The glass containers were fully sealed except for two gas out­
lets, one of which was connected to a Tedlar® gas bag for biogas 
collection (Tedlar Bag, CEL Scientific Corp., Cerritos, CA, USA), and the 
other had a tube reaching the sludge at the bottom of the reactor for 
nitrogen gas flushing and microaeration.
To begin, 0.60 g of PL and 1.64 g of WS were placed into each reactor 
with 100 mL of the evenly mixed inoculum sludge to reach a C/N ratio of 
25 for the loaded substrate and a VSinoculum/VSsubstrate ratio of 1 as 
suggested by previous research [9]. The total substrate TS and VS were 
2.13 g and 1.85 g, respectively. Deionized water was added to obtain a 
total working volume of 200 mL in each reactor, which led to a substrate 
TS of 2.13% and VS of 18.48 g/L (100 mL). The digestion duration (40 
days) was determined by substrate degradation under the selected TS 
level (2.13%), which is lower than in our previous study (4–12%) and 
resulted in faster completion of methane production. This TS was chosen 
to maintain a balanced C/N ratio and a VSinoculum/VSsubstrate ratio of 1, 
ensuring stable and comparable conditions across all treatments. Each 
reactor was then purged with nitrogen for 5 min to remove oxygen from 
the liquid. The reactors were all housed in an incubator at 35 ± 2 ◦C 
mesophilic conditions and run to ferment methane until no measurable 
biogas was produced. The Co-AD system was mixed manually by 
shaking the reactors twice daily, at intervals of 12 h. The gas bag of each 
reactor for biogas collection was replaced daily. The collected gas was 
measured in volume and analyzed for methane content to determine 
methane production.
Cumulative methane yield (CMY, NmL CH4/VSadded) in each reactor 
was calculated through successive summation of daily methane yield 
normalized to the initial VS loading from the initial day to the corre­
sponding operational day. Specific methane yield (SMY, NmL CH4/g 
VSadded) was determined as the final CMY upon cessation of significant 
methane generation. Upon completion of the batch Co-AD process, 
digestate samples were collected from each reactor for physicochemical 
characterization to evaluate the performance of the tested strategies. In 
parallel, sludge samples were also obtained for microbial community 
analysis.

2.4.2. Biogas analysis
The produced biogas in the daily replaced bags was sampled for 
composition analysis using a Shimadzu Gas Chromatograph (GC 2014, 
Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Inc., Maryland, CO, USA) equipped 
with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a ShinCarbon column

Shen J, et.al (2017) [28]. The volume of the biogas produced daily was 
measured using a wet gas test meter (Model XMF-1, Shanghai Cixi In­
strument Co., Ltd, China), whose value was then normalized before 
being used for calculation [29].
2.5. Kinetic study
2.5.1. Kinetic models
The methane yield kinetics of the Co-AD process were characterized 
using four established mathematical models to determine the optimal 
fit: the first-order kinetic model (FM), the modified Gompertz model 
(MGM), the cone model (CNM), and the transfer model (TM). FM (Eq. 
(3)) was first described by Llabr´es-Luengo P, et.al (1987) [30], who 
assumed that hydrolysis was the rate-limiting step that governed the 
overall process [31,32]. MGM (Eq. (4)) was first used to predict methane 
production rate in a batch digester corresponding to the specific growth 
rate of methanogenic bacteria [33], and later became a widely used 
empirical regression model that described cell density in terms of 
exponential growth rates and lag phase duration and could be used to 
identify the maximum methane production potential and lag phase [34]. 
CNM (Eq. (5)) has been used as an empirical model to estimate the 
methane yield rate and the maximum cumulative methane yield, 
showing better fitting performance than other models in methane pro­
duction from Co-AD [35,36]. TM (Eq. (6)) was also used to fit the 
methane production data from anaerobic co-digestion processes [37].

2.6. Microbial community analysis
DNA extractions were performed using the DNeasy PowerLyzer 
PowerSoil Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD). Polymerase chain reaction 
(PCR) amplification of the fourth and fifth hypervariable (V4-V5) re­
gions of 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) was performed. The specific method 
of performing the microbial community analysis was detailed previously 
[41]. Qiime (V1.7.0, https://qiime.org/scripts/assign_taxonomy.html) 
in the Mothur method (v1.39.5) was performed against the SSUrRNA 
database of SILVA (Release 138.1, https://www.arb-silva.de/)) for 
species annotation. Software, R, was used for statistical analysis of the 
microbial community structure using the relative abundance of each 
taxon based on the identification results of the Operational Taxonomic 
Units (OTUs). The function prediction analysis of the microbial com­
munity of the sludge samples was performed according to the 16S rRNA 
sequencing data using PICRUSt2, which is a bioinformatics software 
package (https://github.com/picrust/picrust2/wik) for metagenomic 
function prediction based on the marker gene (16S rRNA in this study). 
The Metacyc database was referenced, which is a collection of a series of 
metabolic pathways and enzymes based on the Kyoto Encyclopedia of 
Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database.
2.7. Cost and benefit analysis based on anaerobic sequencing batch 
reactor framework
Cost and benefit analysis was conducted by estimating the additional 
cost needed for the applied enhancing strategy and the gains in energy 
benefit brought by enhanced methane generation. This study used a 
framework of ASBR for continuous Co-AD to estimate the cost and 
benefit balance in a long-term operation based on a previous study [41]. 
In the previous study, an ASBR with a working volume of 16 L was 
operated at an OLR of 3.8 g VS/Lreactor/day under steady-state condi­
tions following successful startup.
In the current study of a batch experiment, micro-aeration was 
manually conducted, and the cost was difficult to estimate. However, an 
air pump (Uniclife Air Pump UL40, Uniclife @ Amazon.com) was used 
for continuous operation [42], and the cost could be calculated based on 
the electricity consumed since micro-aeration was a continuous process 
together with ongoing substrate loading. We proposed a working vol­
ume of 16 L, with an OLR of 4 g TS/Lreactor/day. A 12 W air pump and a 
flow rate of 0.75 LPH (Litter per hour) were used for microaeration, 
achieving a microaeration rate of 2 mL air /g TS/day. The local elec­
tricity price was $0.1067/kWh. The electric cost by microaeration was 
estimated as $2.4*10−4/day for a continuous operation using an ASBR.
Biochar and nanoparticles were supplemented as a single addition 
and could potentially be reused or recycled across multiple batch cycles. 
The cost was estimated as a one-time expense for each additive. The bulk 
prices for biochar and nanoparticles were $3/kg and $100/kg, respec­
tively. The dosage of biochar and nanoparticles was 1.07 g/Lreactor and 
0.02 g/Lreactor based on reactor working volume, respectively. As a 
result, the costs of biochar and nanoparticles were $3.20*10−3/Lreactor 
and $3.20*10−3/Lreactor, respectively. However, the effective lifetime of 
biochar and nanoparticles depends on their intrinsic properties and the 
solids retention time (SRT) of the reactor. In this study, the SRT (ranging 
from 30 to 360 days in increments of 30 days) was used to represent the

3.1. Performance of the anaerobic co-digestion (Co-AD)
3.1.1. Biomethane generation potential
The profiles of biogas production and the corresponding methane 
content in different groups are shown in Fig. S2. The temporal evolution 
of CMY (NmL CH4/g VSadded) and the final SMY (NmL CH4/g VSadded) 
across different experimental groups are presented in Fig. 1(a, b), 
respectively. All enhancement strategies achieved significantly higher 
SMY (p < 0.05) compared to the control, confirming that M, B, N, and 
their combinations enhanced methane yield from the Co-AD process. 
The B+N treatment achieved the highest SMY (324.8 ± 3.8 NmL CH4/g 
VSadded), representing an 18.4% improvement over the control. The 
treatments B, M+B, M+N, and M+B+N demonstrated the second- 
highest tier of performance, followed by N and M, which exhibited

Among single-strategy treatments, B yielded the highest SMY (304.7 
± 0.4 NmL CH4/g VSadded, p < 0.05), corresponding to an 11.0% 
enhancement relative to the control. M and N showed comparatively 
lower improvements of 7.1% and 8.2%, respectively. The superior per­

colonization substrate, i.e., a conductive matrix facilitating DIET and an 
adsorbent for inhibitory compounds.
For combined treatments, the B+N strategy achieved significantly 
higher SMY than either B or N alone, indicating positive synergistic 
interactions. This synergy likely arises from complementary mecha­
nisms, i.e., biochar provides structural support and conductive surfaces 
for the growth of microbial consortia, while nanoparticles supply 
bioavailable trace elements essential for methanogenic enzymes and 
enhance electron shuttling. The integration of these functions creates an 
optimized microenvironment that simultaneously addresses multiple 
metabolic bottlenecks. Conversely, M+B and M+N showed no signifi­
cant improvement over B and N alone (p > 0.05), indicating the absence 
of synergistic interactions between microaeration and the other treat­
ments. The inability of microaeration to further improve SMY when 
combined with B or N may could reflect a mechanistic overlap, in which 
biochar and nanoparticles had already optimized electron transfer and 
substrate availability, rendering additional oxygen input redundant or 
even inhibitory. Notably, M+B+N exhibited significantly lower SMY 
than B+N, demonstrating antagonistic rather than synergistic effects. 
This antagonism may result from oxygen-induced inhibition of obligate 
anaerobes, competitive metabolism by facultative aerobes, disrupted 
electron flow, and/or oxidative passivation of nanoparticles.

electron transfer capabilities [61,63,64].
In addition, Methanosaeta exhibited a progressive increase in relative 
abundance from the C to the single-treatment groups and further to the 
combined treatments (M+B, M+N, and M+B+N), reaching its highest 
level in the B+N group (dark red). Methanobacterium also increased 
across all treatment groups compared with C, with more pronounced 
enrichment observed in the B-amended groups (B, M+B, and B+N). The 
clear separation between C and enhanced treatments demonstrated that 
enhancement strategies fundamentally altered community structure 
through multiple mechanisms, as mentioned previously. These findings 
indicated that strategic enhancement combinations created functionally 
diverse microbial communities that substantially improved Co-AD sys­
tem performance. The synergistic effects observed in the combined 
treatments suggest optimization of syntrophic relationships between 
fermentative bacteria, syntrophic acetogens, and methanogenic 
archaea, thereby potentially enhancing the overall efficiency and sta­
bility of the Co-AD process.
The heatmap analysis further supports the differences between B+N 
and M+B+N. The B+N group showed relatively higher abundance of 
key methanogens (e.g., Methanosaeta and Methanobacterium) and syn­
trophic/electroactive bacteria (e.g., Syntrophobacter), which are associ­
ated with efficient methane production and electron transfer. In 
contrast, the M+B+N group exhibited a shift toward a more dispersed 
community with relatively lower enrichment of these functional taxa 
and increased abundance of other genera less directly linked to meth­
anogenesis. These patterns suggest that M may alter microbial in­
teractions and weaken the syntrophic relationships established in B+N, 
which is consistent with the observed reduction in methane production, 
although the mechanism remains indicative rather than conclusive.
3.3.3. Archaeal community and predictive methanogenic pathways analysis
Archaea, though representing a minor fraction of the total commu­
nity (approximately 0.8–2.0% relative abundance), exhibited substan­
tial compositional and functional variations in response to the 
enhancement strategies (Fig. 4 (a)). The sludge at the initial sludge (O) 
and the control (C) harbored relatively low archaeal abundances 
(approximately 0.8–0.9%), dominated by Methanosaeta and Meth­
anobacterium, representing the baseline methanogenic capacity. Single- 
amendment treatments (M, B, N) showed moderate increases in total 
archaeal abundance (1.0–1.5%), with M and B particularly enriching 
Methanosaeta, consistent with the genus-level patterns observed in Fig. 3
(b). Notably, the combined enhancement treatments (M+B, B+N, M+N, 
M+B+N) achieved the highest archaeal abundances (1.5–2.0%), with 
M+B and B+N treatments showing the most substantial enrichment. The 
dominance of Methanosaeta across all enhanced treatments, which 
increased progressively from single to combined amendments, confirms 
the preferential stimulation of acetoclastic methanogenesis, which is the 
primary methane production pathway in AD systems [58,59,65].

3.4. Cost-benefit analysis
The estimates of the costs and benefits from the energy values of the 
batch reactors and the assumed continuous ASBR in each group are 
summarized in Table 5. The net benefit value can be calculated by 
subtracting the added cost from the total estimated value of energy 
production. Therefore, the increased values of the treatment groups with 
enhancing techniques compared to C were used to demonstrate whether 
the enhanced energy production could make up for the added cost from 
those techniques. In the batch-scale experiments (200 mL working vol­
ume, 1.85 g VS), all enhancement strategies improved SMY relative to 
the control (274.4 NmL/g VS), with increases ranging from 7.1% for M 
alone (293.9 NmL/g VS) to 18.4% for the B+N (324.8 NmL/g VS). The 
corresponding Ep and Vp followed similar trends, with the B+N 
achieving the highest energy value (1.1 ×10⁻⁴ $/g VS) among all groups. 
When scaled up to a continuous ASBR framework (16 L working volume, 
3.8 g VS/L_reactor/day OLR), the enhanced methane production trans­
lated to substantial increases in total daily energy production. B+N 
achieved the highest methane production (19.7 L/day) and energy value 
(6.6 ×10⁻³ $/day), representing an 18% improvement in volumetric 
methane production compared to C.

distinct economic trajectories for different enhancement strategies as a 
function of operational time (Fig. S3). Initially, all enhancement treat­
ments showed a negative increase in net benefits due to upfront in­
vestment costs, with the triple amendment (M+B+N) exhibiting the 
most pronounced deficit (approximately -$0.08) at day 30. However, as 
operational time extended, the cumulative energy gains progressively 
offset the added costs. The B+N treatment demonstrated the steepest 
positive trajectory, reaching break-even around day 120 and achieving 
the highest net benefit ($0.29) by day 360, attributable to its superior 
methane production enhancement combined with the absence of 
continuous biochar replenishment costs in this scenario. B showed the 
second-best long-term economic performance, reaching approximately 
$0.17 net benefit at day 360, while N achieved $0.13. M treatments (M, 
M+N, M+B) clustered together with modest net benefits ($0.04–0.08 by 
day 360), as their lower operational costs were offset by more moderate 
performance improvements. Notably, the triple amendment (M+B+N) 
showed recovery from its initial deficit but remained below B+N and B 
alone, suggesting that the incremental benefit of combining all three 
strategies did not justify the cumulative costs. This outcome aligns with 
the microbial community analysis (Figs. 3–4), where M+B+N showed 
similar community structure and archaeal enrichment to B+N, indi­
cating redundancy in enhancement mechanisms.
The break-even analysis reveals critical decision points for practical 
implementation, i.e., M becomes economically favorable almost imme­
diately due to negligible costs, B requires approximately 90–120 days of 
operation to recover costs, and N shows intermediate payback periods of 
60–90 days. For short-term operations (<180 days), M or N amendments 
offer the best cost-effectiveness, while for long-term installations (>180 
days), B+N provides superior net economic benefits. The diverging 
trajectories after day 180 (Fig. S3) underscore the importance of oper­
ational planning, i.e., industrial-scale continuous digesters with multi- 
year operational horizons would benefit most from B+N implementa­
tion, potentially achieving net benefits exceeding $100–200 annually 
per cubic meter of reactor volume, whereas pilot-scale or seasonal op­
erations might favor low-cost M strategies.
3.5. Limitations and perspectives
Microbial community analysis was performed without biological 
replication. Therefore, statistical comparisons among treatments were 
not conducted. As a result, subtle differences, particularly for low- 
abundance taxa, should be interpreted with caution, and the observed 
trends are presented as supportive rather than definitive evidence. 
Future studies incorporating biological replication and statistical anal­
ysis are recommended to validate the observed community shifts.
Although strong correlations between methanogen abundance and 
methane production were observed in this study, substrate conversion 
efficiency would depend not only on microbial abundance but also on 
functional gene expression and enzymatic activities. While the current 
microbial community analysis focused on taxonomic composition, 
future work should use metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics to 
directly assess functional activity. For example, functional gene profiling 
targeting key metabolic pathways would directly link community 
structure to metabolic capacity; co-occurrence network analysis and 
metabolite tracking could elucidate syntrophic interactions between 
community members. Spatial distribution analysis, particularly exam­
ining microbial colonization on biochar surfaces versus bulk liquid, 
would reveal microhabitat preferences.
The involvement of mechanisms such as DIET and M-enhanced hy­
drolysis in this study is inferred from indirect evidence, including pro­
cess performance, kinetic parameters, and relative shifts in microbial 
community composition. While the enrichment of potential electro­
active microorganisms and methanogens, together with improved 
methane production kinetics, may suggest conditions favorable for 
DIET, these observations are not sufficient for definitive confirmation, 
particularly given the overall similarity in community structures across 
treatments. Therefore, the proposed mechanisms should be considered 
plausible but not conclusive. Advanced analytical approaches, such as 
electrochemical characterization, functional gene analysis, or tran­
scriptomics, are required to directly verify these processes in future 
studies.
Due to the low oxygen dosage and the high oxygen uptake capacity 
of anaerobic microorganisms and reduced intermediates, the introduced 
oxygen was expected to be rapidly consumed rather than accumulated in 
the system. However, dissolved oxygen (DO), oxidation-reduction po­
tential (ORP), or gas-phase oxygen concentrations were not directly 
monitored in this study. Therefore, the oxygen dynamics could not be 
quantitatively assessed. Future work incorporating direct measurements 
of DO, ORP, or oxygen profiles is needed to characterize oxygen 
behavior better and validate the micro-aeration conditions. In addition, 
this study was conducted under dilute conditions with TS at 2.13%.

Industrial systems are typically operated at < 15% TS (wet AD) or 
> 15% TS (dry AD) [68], where mass transfer limitations, microbial 
dynamics, and potential ammonia inhibition differ substantially. Sys­
tematic evaluation across varying TS levels is needed to establish 
operational windows and optimize dosing strategies for different 
application scenarios. Batch reactors employed here have enabled 
fundamental performance assessment but do not capture challenges of 
continuous operation, including process stability under dynamic 
loading, shock load resilience, and long-term enhancement effects.
It should be noted that the techno-economic assessment was based 
on a simulated continuously operated ASBR system and is intended to 
provide a comparative evaluation rather than a precise prediction of 
full-scale performance. To ensure consistency, several simplifying as­
sumptions were applied, including the single addition of B and N at 
startup, which was supported by biochar's recalcitrance and long-term 
stability as a microbial carrier [69] and the chemical stability of Fe3O4 
nanoparticles [70]. While the magnetic properties of Fe₃O₄ suggest 
feasibility for recovery via magnetic separation, the recovery efficiency, 
material loss, and long-term stability were not experimentally validated. 
In practical continuous systems, both B and N may undergo degradation, 
attrition, or washout, requiring periodic replenishment, which would 
increase operational costs and potentially affect the relative economic 
performance of all amended systems. Therefore, the results should be 
interpreted with caution. Conversely, potential cost reductions through 
bulk purchasing of N or in-situ B production from waste biomass could 
further improve economic viability. Future studies incorporating 
experimental validation of material recovery, stability, and continuous 
operation data are needed to improve the robustness and practical 
relevance of the techno-economic assessment.
The findings of this study highlighted the importance of strategy 
selection and interaction effects in optimizing Co-AD process perfor­
mance. While the B+N combination showed the most favorable results 
under the tested conditions, the observed antagonistic effect in the 
M+B+N system suggested that overlapping or competing mechanisms 
may limit synergistic benefits. Future studies should further investigate 
these interactions using advanced analytical techniques (e.g., electro­
chemical characterization and functional gene analysis) to better resolve 
underlying mechanisms. In addition, validation under continuous or 
pilot-scale systems, along with consideration of material stability, re­
covery, and long-term operation, will be critical to translating these 
findings into practical applications.
Besides, substrate-specific responses require further investigation, as 
lignocellulosic materials may exhibit different responses to M due to 
their recalcitrant structures, while lipid-rich substrates could benefit 
more from B’s capacity to mitigate long-chain VFA inhibition. 
Comprehensive evaluation across diverse substrate portfolios would 
establish the generalizability of these enhancement strategies and help 
develop substrate-specific optimization protocols. Future research pri­
orities should include multi-factorial optimization approaches employ­
ing response surface methodology or machine learning algorithms, 
investigation of functionalized materials such as magnetic biochar and 
alternative nanoparticles, and integration with complementary pre- 
treatment technologies (thermal, enzymatic). Finally, pilot-scale vali­
dation to comprehensively assess methane production, digestate quality, 
greenhouse gas emissions, and environmental impacts is essential to 
ensure holistic sustainability and facilitate technology transfer to full- 
scale industrial implementation.
4. Conclusions
This study systematically evaluated M, B, and N amendments for 
enhancing the Co-AD of PL with WS. All strategies improved SMY 
compared to the control (274.4 NmL CH₄/g VS), with B+N achieving the 
highest performance (324.8 ± 3.8 NmL CH4/g VS, +18.4%). B+N also 
achieved superior solids removal (80.2% TS, 86.3% VS). Kinetic 
modeling revealed distinct mechanisms, i.e., M increased k by 12.0% 
and Rm by 19.5%, B enhanced Ym, while N shortened λ to 0.72–0.74 
days. Microbial community analysis demonstrated that all strategies 
enriched the acetoclastic methanogen Methanosaeta, with B+N 
achieving the highest abundance. Mechanistically, M enriched hydro­
lytic bacteria enhancing substrate degradation, B facilitated DIET and 
microbial colonization while enriching syntrophic bacteria, and N sup­
plied trace elements and promoted DIET. Cost-benefit analysis showed 
that B+N achieved the highest long-term net benefit ($0.29 after 360 
days) with break-even at 90–120 days, making it optimal for long-term 
installations, while M was suited for short-term operations. Overall, 
B+N is recommended as the optimal enhancement strategy. This study 
provides mechanistic insights into synergistic microbial-material in­
teractions and establishes an integrated framework for process optimi­
zation to pave the way for industrial-scale AD proliferation. Future 
validation under diverse operational conditions, multi-omics in­
vestigations, and pilot-scale sustainability assessments are necessary for 
advancing the circular bioeconomy through improved waste 
valorization.
